was felt that keeping with the change in time, keeping with the fact that no 
longer was Mumbai a pre-eminent place for departure of Hajis, the Central Haj 
Committee Bill or rather the Haj Committee Act would have to be replaced by 
the Central Haj Committee Bill, 2000. This Bill would then seek to correct some 
of the inconsistencies and imbalances that are in place in the existing Act of 
1959. This Bill was placed before the House in 2000. It was presented or 
rather referred to the Standing Committe e on External Affairs. That Committee 
made certain recommendations In fact, they made 23 recommendations for 
alterations to be made to the Bill as it has been presented. I am pleased to 
say, Mr. Vice-Chairman, Sir, that out 23 recommendations, 22 
recommendations have been accepted in toto. One recommendation has been 
accepted partially and that was the re commendation about the shift or rather 
the original Bill of 2000 suggested that  the Central Haj Committee office be 
shifted from Bombay to Delhi in keeping with the move of emphasis away from 
Mumbai and that regional offices be opened. The Government of India, after 
considering this fact, felt because the infrastructure and an enormous Central 
Haj Committee office was already in place in Mumbai, it would be pointless to 
reconstruct a similar office in Delhi and then infrastructure that is already in 
place in Mumbai would go waste. Also, as far as regional offices were 
concerned, it was felt that as of ri ght now, the State Haj Committees were 
doing an excellent job. It was not necessary to have regional offices of the 
Central Haj Committee in various States . But that provision has been kept 
open, and, in case, that need is felt ne cessary, we would get into that as and 
when the need arises. 
Then, the number of pilgrims has increased dramatically, from 24,000 
in 1992 to 72,000 in the year 2002. Along with this, the Central Government, 
working with the Central Haj Committee, has also endeavoured to transfer a lot 
of their responsibilities for the arrangem ents in the run up to the Haj to the 
various State Haj Committees. For example, the draw of lots by which pilgrims 
are selected, or the qura, earlier, was the responsibility of the Central Haj 
Committee, carried out in Mumbai. .This responsibility has gradually   been   
transferred   to   the   State   Haj   Cdmmittees.      The   pre- 
258 

RAJYA SABHA [8 May, 2002] 
embarkation arrangements, tr ansportation to the embarkation points, provision 
camps, and facilities at such points, all these arrangements have gradually been 
transferred to the State Haj Committees be cause it is felt that the State Haj 
Committees being on the ground right there, will be able to make better 
arrangements. Of course, in a supportive capacity, the Central Haj Committee 
and the Ministry of External Affairs continue to work. A number of Members who 
participated in this debate had made a refe rence to the fact that the Central Haj 
Committee has no role to play. Once the Hajis leave India and reach Saudi 
Arabia the Central Haj Committee has no role to play in the selection of 
accommodation. As a result, sub-standard accommodation is chosen or there is 
some amount of financial impropriety in  the selection of residential units in 
Mecca and Madina. Now, first and foremost, every effort is made to maintain a 
transparent system in the selection of accommodation. The guidelines for 
selection of accommodation are laid down  by the Government of Saudi Arabia, 
in terms of the amount of space to be ma de available. This year, the amount of 
space for the Hajis was increased from 2.5 sq. me ters to 3 sq. meters. Aside 
from that, the guidelines of the Ministry of External Affairs to our officials in 
Saudi Arabia and the accommodation teams that visit there are that no building 
without lift and telephone will be taken on rent for Hajis. To suggest that the 
Central Haj Committee has no role to play in this, is incorrect because what 
happens is, the accommodation is selected jointly by teams of the Central Haj 
Committee as well as officials of the Consulate General of India. For this 
purpose, building selection teams ar e deputed. The State Haj Committee 
officials also go to Mecca. They select buildings as per the pre-set norms for this 
purpose. Rooms are measured. Buildings are taken on the basis of the number 
of pilgrims. As I mentioned, no buildings are taken without lift or telephone 
facility, and they must fall within the prescribed distance from Harin Sharief. 
After the buildings are identified, a me mber of the Haj Committee visits Mecca 
Sharief and goes through each of these selections, visits each of the buildings, 
ensures that - the guidelines  that are laid down are being followed, and makes 
sure that the Hajis get the best possible accommodation. Wherever problem 
arises with the accommodation, is  not with the pre-set numbers of Hajis, for 
which the officials in Saudi Arabia receive prior notice. It is when at the last 
minute, sometimes, the * Central Haj Committee sends people from the waiting 
list, and, within a few days' notice, a sks our officials in Mecca and Madina to 
make accommodation available, then we have to settle for a lower category of 
accommodation because, otherwise, we are accused of 
259 

[8 May, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
not making facilities available. But, if prior information is made available to the 
Government officials by the Centra l Haj Committee, then, accommodation, 
within the prescribed norms, is made available to the Hajis. As far as the 
financial impropriety of bungling in financ ial transactions is concerned, it has 
been the effort of this Government, of my Ministry, working alongside with our 
counterparts in the Saudi Government, to  ensure that each contract that is 
signed with landlords by the Government, a copy of that is made available to 
the Haj Ministry in the Kingdom of Saudi  Arabia. The purpose of this is that 
each of these contracts is vetted. If necessary, it is investigated. And, if the 
Saudi Government feels that there has  been some sort of impropriety or 
financial bungling, they get into the act themselves. A distinguished Member 
from Andhra Prradesh, in the course of his maiden speech, if I am not 
mistaken, made a suggestion that t he Vigilance Commission could, perhaps, 
somehow, be involved in this. I believe, Mr. Vice Chairman, this is a very good 
suggestion. This is a suggestion that my Ministry will be happy to consider. 
And we will certainly look into this possibility, whereby the Vigilance 
Commission or the Vigilance Department of the Ministry of External Affairs can 
have oversight facilities into the func tioning of the Haj Committee as well as 
into the financial dealings, and also the accommodation and other 
arrangements that are made with regard to the Haj. I am sure this may be a 
solution the allegations that are made  about financial impropriety and other 
bunglings that are supposed to go on during the course of the Haj. 
As far as accommodation at Madina is concerned, this is not 
something that is done by the Government or by our officials. The building 
selection teams in Madina are sent by the Central Haj Committee, and they 
are responsible for selection of the acco mmodation. In fact, most of the time, 
accommodation at Madina is not a proble m. If I am not mistaken, a number of 
pilgrims in the last Haj, in fact, stayed in three or four-star hotels for Saudi 
Riyal 200 only, which is, I think, an excellent deal for the Hajis to be able to 
stay there for the period that they are there. 
A reference was made to the effect that, perhaps, Air India is cross-
subsidising itself through the Haj busi ness that they do. It was suggested that 
commercial tickets are available for Rs. 27,000/- whereas the rate that Air 
India charged this year was $700, wh ich works out to Rs. 33,600/-. Hon. 
Members must remember that in commercia l flights, they have  traffic in both 
directions. On a commercial flight, they pick up passengers in Delhi and fly 
them to Jeddah.   The same plane comes back, 
260 

RAJYA SABHA [8 May, 2002] 
with passengers from Jeddah to Delhi. In a chartered flight, they have only 
one-way traffic. It is not possible for them to provide you an aircraft at the 
same ticket cost when, on one direction the plane has to get back empty. This 
is why there is a difference in the cost of rates that are charged by Air India for 
chartered flights, as opposed to the commercial rates that are available for 
those who buy tickets and come separately. 
Why the Central Haj Committee not play a more active role, or rather, 
why does the Central Committee not take over tr^e operation in Saudi Arabia? 
It is a very complicated question. Haj operations are not a two-monthly effort 
in the calendar. The moment the Haj of one year is concluded, the efforts for 
the next year's Haj begin. It is not po ssible for the Central Haj Committee to 
be present in Saudi Arabia continuously. It is not possible for them to have a 
continuous operation of al l the efforts and the prepar ation that need to go in 
for a successful conclusion of a Haj. 
Has this effort or has the current system worked well? I would like to 
believe that it has worked well, and my Ministry also certainly believes so. In 
fact, we have figures to support this. At the end of Haj 2000, the Consul 
General, Jeddah, who looks after a lar ge part of the Haj work, circulated a 
post-Haj survey form to a large number of Hajis; this was not just in English, it 
was in Hindi, Urdu, Malayalam and Tam il also. A large number of responses 
were received. If you look at the responses  that were given, you will find that 
once these were tabulated, only five per cent of the p ilgrims found the 
accommodation at Mecca unsatisfacto ry; only seven per cent found the 
accommodation at Madina unsatisfactory;  5.9 per cent found the staff at 
Mecca uncooperative, and 8.4 per ce nt found the staff at the Airport 
unsatisfactory. Only three per cent found the medical services unsatisfactory. 
Given the overall number of pttgrims and the amount of effort that goes into 
this, I am sure, the House will agree that it is a huge labour of love, and a lot 
of effort goes into ensuring such amount of satisfaction on the part of such a 
large number of Hajis who travel from I ndia to Saudi Arabia. That having been 
said, Mr. Vice Chairman, there is no pl ace for complacency. My Ministry, the 
Government, my officials, in place in Saudi Arabia, in fact, the Central Haj 
Committee and the State Haj Committees - our consistent and constant effort 
is to improve year in, year out, the Haj arrangements. Every year, we learn 
from our experiences, from the mistak es that we have made and seek to 
improve on them. Some of the lessons that we have learnt previously, that is, 
in the year 2000-2002, we corrected.   Those who have 
261 

 [8 May, 2002] RAJYA SABHA 
been for Haj will know that on arrival in Jeddah, where, earlier they used to  be 
given bank drafts, they had to wait in lines at the banks for 6-7 hours in order to 
convert those  bank drafts into S audi  Riyals.  From this year,  i.e. 2002 Haj, 
what was done was that with bank counters open at the  airports in India itself, 
Saudi Riyals were handed over to Hajis in order to  spare them that 6-8 hours' 
wait at the' airport in Saudi Arabia.   Aside from this, there have been problems 
with luggage. One of the hon. Members mentioned that Hajis are not allowed to 
fly back with their aab-e-zum-zum.  This, I must admit, Mr. Vice-Chairman, Sir, 
caught me by surprise, because  upto 10 litres of aab-e-zum-zum is allowed to 
be carried by all Hajis in their accompanied baggage,    oo, there is no question 
of the aab-e-zum-zum  coming at a later stage.  What happens is that when 
their baggage exceeds  the approved limit, then the excess baggage comes 
later in cargo flights,  but  aab-e-zum-zum comes  as an accompanied  
baggage.     In  fact,  the   airlines have aab-e-zum-zum  bottles on the flight to 
be given to those pilgrims, who have for some reason either misplaced this or 
have not been able to carry any aab-e-zum-zum in the flight with them.   One of 
the hon. Members made reference to t he fact that why should an ex-officio 
member, not be a non-muslim.     Mr.  Vice-Chairman,  Sir,  the simple fact  is 
that ex-officio  members of the Central  Haj Committee are required to go to  
Mecca Sharief, Madina Sharief in con nection with the arrangements that are to 
be made there,, and, as we all know, Saudi law prohibits non-Muslims  from 
entering the municipal limits of Mecca Sharief and Madina Sharief. Therefore, if 
w e  w e r e  t o  h a v e  n o n - M u s l i m  a s  ex-officio members, I am sure,  the House 
would understand that it would be a hindrance to their being  able to carry out 
their activities, as they would not be allowed to enter the  two main cities where 
their activities would have to be carried out.   Aside from this, suggestions were 
made about investments to be made by the  Central Haj Committee.   This is a 
very good suggestion.   The avenues for  investments and where these 
investments can be made, can be taken up by  the Central Haj Committee, 
once the by-laws have been agreed.    If you  have read the Bill that we are 
seeking to pass today, the by-laws of the  Central Haj Committee will be 
decided only once Parliament agrees the Haj  Committee Bill.   This is exactly 
why there are a number of open areas that  Members talked about, areas with 
regard to selection of ex-officio  members, investment areas, etc.    One hon. 
Member asked how it is that the zonal  representatives  will   be  selected   for   
representation   in  the  Central   Haj Committee.   Mr. Vice-Chairman, Sir, I am 
sorry, I stand corrected. The E.O.  on my notes which I took for ex-officio,  
actually means Executive Officer.

RAJYA SABHA [8 May, 2002] 
So, it is the Executive Officers who will  have to be Muslims, so that they can 
travel to Mecca and Madina Sharief. Even now, as I was saying the question 
was asked as to how zonal representatives would be selected for inclusion in 
the Central Haj Committe. All this will be agreed upon when bylaws are 
drafted, and as I said, the by-laws will be drafted once this Bill is passed by 
Parliament. So, Mr. Vice-Chairman, Sir, wi th this, without seeking to take too 
much time or rather more time of t he House, I would like to thank all the 
Members for participating in this debate, for their very valuable suggestions. 
We will, in future, also seek to incorporate as many suggestions as possible 
into actions of the Government, and the Central Haj Committee, because, 
ultimately, our endeavour is to ensure the smoothest possible Haj for all the 
Hajis who go from here. With these word s, Mr. Vice-Chairman, Sir, I would 
request this House to pass this Bill.
